strengths: Addresses an important and emerging problem: visual hallucination snowballing in multi-agent VLM systems caused by over-reliance on textual communication.
Provides insightful empirical observations regarding turn-wise visual attention degradation, specifically identifying the decline of middle-layer unimodal vision tokens.
Extensive experimental evaluation across four multi-agent topologies, ten model variants, and diverse vision-language benchmarks showing consistent gains.
weaknesses: The method requires introducing and training an auxiliary lightweight transformer block, making it less purely plug-and-play than purely inference-time interventions.
The token selection and attention reallocation mechanism depends on multiple heuristics and sensitive hyperparameters (e.g., peak salience threshold, reallocation coefficients).
The newly introduced Hallucination Snowballing (HS) metric relies heavily on closed-source LLM-as-a-judge scoring, which may introduce evaluation variance.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes the practical problem of visual hallucination snowballing across turns in visual multi-agent systems.
Provides intuitive empirical analyses linking multi-agent degradation to the decline of visual attention allocation in middle transformer layers.
Conducts extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks, agent communication topologies, and model families.
weaknesses: The boundary between multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing and generic multi-turn error propagation or context drift remains somewhat blurred.
The method introduces engineering complexity via additional token contextualization modules and manual layer-wise attention reallocation.
The newly proposed Hallucination Snowballing (HS) metric relies heavily on closed-source LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, which may introduce subjective bias.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practical challenge: multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing caused by textual relay.
Provides insightful empirical analysis linking multi-turn visual attention degradation to unimodal peak tokens in middle layers.
Extensive experimental validation across multiple architectures, base VLMs up to 34B parameters, and various benchmark types.
weaknesses: The overall performance gains on standard comprehensive benchmarks are relatively modest (typically 1-3%).

strengths: Timely and relevant problem formulation: The paper tackles multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing, an increasingly prominent issue as multi-modal large language models are deployed in collaborative multi-agent systems.

Insightful requisite analyses: The authors provide fine-grained turn-, layer-, and token-wise attention diagnostics across multiple VLM architectures, demonstrating that visual attention degrades significantly in middle layers across extended agent turns and identifying the key role of unimodal vision tokens.

Extensive experimental evaluation: Experiments span 8 comprehensive and hallucination-specific benchmarks, 4 MAS communication topologies (linear, layered, random, circular), and 10 base models ranging from 7B to 34B parameters.
Practical considerations for modern architectures: The inclusion of a Key-Norm alternative to attention-score-based selection ensures applicability to models utilizing FlashAttention.
weaknesses: Ambiguity regarding 'plug-and-play' versus training requirements: The main text repeatedly claims ViF is a 'lightweight, plug-and-play mitigation paradigm' (Abstract, Section 1, Section 3). However, Table 8 in the Appendix reveals a two-stage training recipe where the LLM is trainable in Stage 2. This creates an unfair comparison against purely training-free decoding/inference baselines (e.g., DeCo, VISTA, FarSight) unless clarified.

Under-specified multi-agent benchmarking setup: It is unclear how standard single-turn VQA benchmarks (e.g., POPE, MME, HallBench) are converted into extended multi-turn interactions spanning up to 20 turns (as shown in Figure 2 and Figure 7). The exact agent prompts, conversational protocols, and termination criteria need clearer exposition in the main text.

Uncertainty around the Hallucination Snowballing (HS) metric: The proposed HS metric (Equation 7) depends on an LLM judge score $h$, but details regarding prompt formulation, variance, and consistency across multiple turns are insufficiently validated.
Incomplete text in the abstract: The abstract contains an unfinished sentence at the end ('The source code will be available at: ').

strengths: Novel and timely problem formulation: The paper tackles multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing, an increasingly prominent failure mode where early visual misinterpretations amplify across multi-turn VLM agent interactions.

Comprehensive empirical analysis: The layer-wise, turn-wise, and token-wise attention analyses provide compelling empirical justification for the method, identifying that attention to vision tokens significantly degrades in middle layers across turns and highlighting the importance of unimodal peak tokens.

Extensive experimental evaluation: The proposed method is evaluated across 10 VLM backbones (ranging from 7B to 34B), four multi-agent topologies (linear, layered, random, circular), and eight standard vision-language and hallucination benchmarks.
Practical accommodation for FlashAttention: Providing a Key-Norm approximation for token selection makes the approach viable for modern architectures where attention weights are not materialized.

Strong comparative results against single-agent baselines: Demonstrates clearly that existing single-agent hallucination mitigation techniques degrade or fail to prevent snowballing in multi-turn multi-agent settings, whereas the proposed visual flow approach maintains performance across agent turns.
weaknesses: Contradiction regarding 'plug-and-play' claims and training overhead: The paper repeatedly frames ViF as a 'plug-and-play' mitigation paradigm, yet Section D.1 and Table 8 describe a two-stage training procedure (pre-training and instruction tuning) where the Transformer Block, Projector, and even the Large Language Model are trainable. The paper lacks details on the training datasets used and does not adequately clarify how this can be considered plug-and-play compared to purely training-free decoding baselines.

Underspecified multi-agent task execution across turns: The paper does not clearly specify how standard single-turn VLM benchmarks (such as POPE, AMBER, or MMBench) are formulated into multi-turn MAS workflows (e.g., up to 20 turns in Figure 7). The exact prompts, communication protocols, and agent role prompts across turns should be detailed.

Validation of the proposed HS metric: The Hallucination Snowballing (HS) metric relies on a judge model score $h$ and propagation distance $d$, but the paper provides limited details on prompt design, sensitivity, or correlation with human judgments for this newly introduced metric.

Lack of inference runtime and memory overhead analysis: Passing contextualized visual relay tokens increases context length across agent turns, and token selection/attention reallocation adds computational steps. Quantifying wall-clock latency, token count scaling, and GPU memory consumption across turns is missing.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes an important and timely problem: visual hallucination snowballing in multi-agent visual language model systems, where errors propagate and amplify across communication turns.

Provides extensive and insightful empirical analyses across layers, tokens, and turns (Figures 1–5, 10, 11), revealing the degradation of visual attention and highlighting the critical role of middle-layer unimodal vision tokens.

Comprehensive empirical validation across ten base vision-language models (ranging from 7B to 34B parameters), four distinct multi-agent topologies (linear, layered, random, circular), and eight standard benchmarks.
Includes practical design considerations, such as a Key-Norm approximation that allows token selection to work seamlessly when Flash-Attention makes raw attention scores inaccessible.
weaknesses: Ambiguity regarding the 'plug-and-play' claim vs. required training: The method is described as lightweight and plug-and-play, yet Section 3.1 and Table 8 state that contextualizing the relay tokens requires an auxiliary lightweight transformer block trained via a two-stage pipeline (pre-training and instruction tuning). The paper lacks details on the training dataset, compute cost, and whether a new adapter must be trained separately for every base model.

Unclear token accumulation and inference overhead: As visual relay tokens are extracted and fed into subsequent agents across up to 20 turns, it is not sufficiently clarified whether relay tokens accumulate across turns or are replaced per turn, and what the exact latency/memory footprint overhead is during multi-agent inference.

Lack of multi-agent specific baselines: Comparisons in Table 5 focus solely on methods designed for single-agent hallucination mitigation (e.g., MemVR, VISTA, FarSight). Simple multi-agent communication baselines (e.g., re-captioning, image re-prompting/cropping, or debate/verification agents) are missing.

Formal definition and evaluation of the HS metric: Equation 7 introduces the Hallucination Snowballing (HS) metric, but the definition of propagation distance $d_i$ across complex topologies (e.g., circular and random graphs) and the prompt/reliability of the LLM-judge for score $h_i$ need more formal and reproducible specification.
